Students | mokopuna are taught the foundational knowledge and practices of Outdoor
Education, including the relationships between people, place, and te taiao (the
environment), and the knowledge and practices used to participate, lead, make
decisions, and respond effectively in outdoor contexts.

Outdoor Education | Akoranga tū-ā-nuku provides students | mokopuna with the
knowledge and practices to participate safely and effectively in outdoor environments,
including planning and navigation, environmental interpretation, outdoor skills,
leadership, facilitation, and decision-making. This disciplinary knowledge helps
students | mokopuna to develop expertise in analysing outdoor situations, applying
technical and environmental knowledge, and making informed and ethical decisions.
As students | mokopuna progress through Years 12–13, they are taught to develop
the ability to interpret, analyse, and evaluate information from environmental, cultural,
and technical sources in written form. This enables them to communicate informed
judgements and recommendations, justify decisions using evidence, and examine
how participation, governance, stewardship, and leadership influence people, place,
and te taiao.

 Disciplinary Writing

 Focus: the use of writing to reflect the ways in which knowledge is organised, analysed, and communicated within the discipline.

 In Outdoor Education | Akoranga tū-ā-nuku, students use explicitly taught disciplinary writing to record, interpret, analyse, and communicate evidence from outdoor experiences, environmental
 observations, and other relevant sources to explain, justify, and evaluate decisions and actions.

Designing a programme

Toi mokopuna must be woven through the knowledge and practices in each whenu.
The teaching sequence is designed to be taught as a non-linear programme. The
knowledge and practice statements within each element are related, but teachers
may select complementary statements from across the sequence or treat sub-
elements as discrete units of work. Disciplinary writing is most effectively taught when
integrated across the teaching programme. Practical outdoor experiences are
fundamental to the subject, providing the contexts in which students | mokopuna
develop, apply, test, and integrate disciplinary knowledge and practices.
